title: Manage project permissions
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-cloud-administration/docs/manage-project-permissions/
last_updated: 2025-02-18
---
# Manage project permissions

Project permissions control who can see and act on issues in a company-managed project. Each permission is granted to a project role, a group, an application access level, or a single user, and those grants live in the permission scheme that the project uses. Changing a grant affects every project that shares the scheme.

## Before you begin

You need the **Administer Jira** global permission, or the **Administer projects** permission for the project you want to change. Team-managed projects use access roles instead of permission schemes, so the steps below don't apply to them.

## Grant a project permission

1. Go to **Settings** > **Issues** > **Permission schemes**.
2. Find the scheme your project uses and select **Permissions**.
3. Next to the permission you want to change, select **Edit**.
4. Choose who to grant it to (e.g. **Project role**, **Group**, or **Any logged-in user**).
5. Select **Grant**.

Grants take effect immediately, although browser caching can delay what a user sees for up to a minute.

## Remove a project permission

1. Open the permission scheme and select **Permissions**.
2. Next to the grant you want to drop, select **Remove**.
3. Confirm the change.

> **Note:** Removing **Browse projects** from a group removes that group's access to the project's issues, boards, and dashboards, i.e. the project disappears from their project list entirely.

## Troubleshoot permission errors

If someone reports that they can't see an issue they expect to see, check the project's permission scheme first, then check whether an issue security level is restricting the individual issue.

title: What are permission schemes?
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-cloud-administration/docs/manage-permission-schemes/
last_updated: 2025-01-28
---
# What are permission schemes?

A permission scheme is a named set of project permission grants. One scheme can be shared by many company-managed projects, which keeps access rules consistent without repeating the same configuration in every project.

## How permission schemes work

Each scheme lists every project permission (e.g. **Browse projects**, **Create issues**, **Transition issues**) and who holds it. A user gets a permission if any one of its grants applies to them. Grants are additive, i.e. there is no deny rule.

## Before you begin

Creating a scheme requires the **Administer Jira** global permission.

## Create a permission scheme

1. Go to **Settings** > **Issues** > **Permission schemes**.
2. Select **Add permission scheme**.
3. Enter a name and a short description that says which projects it is for.
4. Select **Add**, then select **Permissions** to add grants.

We recommend granting permissions to project roles rather than to named users, so project admins can manage membership themselves.

## Before you begin

Switching a project's scheme changes access for everyone in that project at once. Tell project admins before you do it.

## Associate a scheme with a project

1. Open the project, then go to **Project settings** > **Permissions**.
2. Select **Actions** > **Use a different scheme**.
3. Choose the scheme and select **Associate**.

> **Note:** A project can use exactly one permission scheme at a time. Deleting a scheme is only possible once no project is associated with it.

# Grant the Browse projects permission to a group

**Browse projects** is the permission that lets a user open a project and see its issues, boards, backlog, and dashboards. If a group reports that a project is missing from their project list, this is almost always the permission to check.

## Before you begin

Make sure the group already exists and has members. Groups are managed in **Administration** > **Groups**, not in project settings. The users in the group also need product access to Jira, because a project permission cannot grant access on its own.

## Grant the Browse projects permission {#browse-projects}

1. Go to **Settings** > **Issues** > **Permission schemes**.
2. Select the scheme used by the project.
3. Find **Browse projects** and select **Edit**.
4. Select **Group**, then choose the group from the list.
5. Select **Grant**.

If several projects share the scheme, the group gains browse access to all of them. To limit access to one project, copy the scheme first and associate the copy with that project only.

## Check that the group can see the project

Ask a member of the group to reload their project list, or use **Permission helper** in **Settings** > **Issues** to test a specific user against a specific issue. Permission helper shows each grant that was evaluated and why it passed or failed, which is faster than reading the scheme by hand.

title: What are issue security levels?
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-cloud-administration/docs/configure-issue-security-schemes/
last_updated: 07/02/2025
---
# What are issue security levels?

Issue security levels restrict individual issues to named people, even when everyone in the project has **Browse projects**. Levels are defined in an issue security scheme, which is then associated with a project.

## How issue security differs from project permissions

Project permissions decide what a user can do across a whole project. An issue security level narrows visibility down to a single issue. If an issue has a security level set and the user is not in that level, the issue is hidden from search, boards, and reports, i.e. it behaves as if it does not exist.

## Create an issue security scheme

1. Go to **Settings** > **Issues** > **Issue security schemes**.
2. Select **Add issue security scheme**.
3. Enter a name and description, then select **Add**.

## Add security levels

1. Select **Security levels** next to your scheme.
2. Enter a level name (e.g. `Reporter and approvers only`) and select **Add security level**.
3. Select **Add** in the level's row to choose who it applies to: a project role, a group, the reporter, the assignee, or a user field.

## Set a default level

Select **Default** on a level to apply it to new issues automatically. Users who cannot see the default level can still create issues, but they will lose sight of them after creation, so use a default sparingly.

> **Note:** Users need the **Set issue security** permission to change the level on an issue.

title: Manage global permissions
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-cloud-administration/docs/manage-global-permissions/
last_updated: 2024-12-16
---
# Manage global permissions

Global permissions apply across your whole Jira site rather than to one project. They are granted to groups only, never to individual users.

## Available global permissions

- **Administer Jira** - full administrative access to schemes, fields, and workflows.
- **Browse users and groups** - see user and group pickers when assigning work or sharing filters.
- **Create team-managed projects** - create projects that are configured by their own team.
- **Share dashboards and filters** - share with groups and projects rather than individuals.
- **Manage group filter subscriptions** - create filter subscriptions for other groups.
- **Bulk change** - run bulk edit, move, and transition operations.

## Grant a global permission

1. Go to **Settings** > **System** > **Global permissions**.
2. Under **Grant permission**, choose the permission.
3. Choose the group, then select **Add**.

Keep **Administer Jira** limited to a small, named group. Everyone in that group can change configuration for every project on the site.

## Remove a global permission

1. Open **Global permissions**.
2. Find the row for the permission and group.
3. Select **Delete**, then confirm.

> **Note:** Jira prevents you from removing the last **Administer Jira** grant, so you cannot lock every administrator out of the site.

last_updated: 2025-02-05
---
# Manage project roles

Project roles group people by the job they do in a project, e.g. developers, reviewers, or service desk agents. Roles are defined once for the whole site. Each company-managed project then decides who fills each role. A permission scheme that grants to a role works in every project without naming any users.

## Default project roles

New sites include the **Administrators** role. Products add their own roles as well, e.g. **Service Desk Team** and **Service Desk Customers** in Jira Service Management. You can rename or delete any role except one that a scheme still references.

## Create a project role

1. Go to **Settings** > **System** > **Project roles**.
2. Enter a name and a description.
3. Select **Add project role**.

The new role starts with no members in any project. It has no effect until a permission scheme or notification scheme grants something to it.

## Add people to a project role

1. Open the project, then go to **Project settings** > **People**.
2. Select **Add people**.
3. Search for users or groups, choose a role, and select **Add**.

> **Note:** Adding a group to a role grants the role to everyone in that group, including people who join the group later. Check group membership in **admin.atlassian.com** before you add large groups such as `jira-software-users`.

last_updated: 2025-01-09
---
# Create an issue and a subtask

Issues are the units of work your team tracks in Jira. A subtask breaks an issue into smaller pieces that different people can pick up. Subtasks share the parent issue's project and are listed under the parent.

## Create an issue

1. Select **+ Create** in the top navigation bar.
2. Choose the **Project** and **Issue type** (e.g. **Story**, **Bug**, or **Task**).
3. Enter a **Summary** and fill in any required fields.
4. Select **Create**.

To add several issues one after another, select **Create another** before you select **Create**.

## Create a subtask

1. Open the parent issue.
2. Select **Add a child issue**. The button is a branch icon below the summary.
3. Enter a summary for the subtask and press **Enter**.

You need the **Create issues** project permission to add subtasks. Subtasks must also be enabled for the project's issue type scheme.

## Convert an issue to a subtask

1. Open the issue and select **Actions** (`•••`) > **Convert to subtask**.
2. Choose the parent issue and the subtask issue type.
3. Follow the steps to map status and fields, then select **Convert**.

> **Note:** An issue that already has its own subtasks can't be converted, i.e. Jira supports only one level of subtasks under a standard issue.

title: Use advanced search with Jira Query Language (JQL)
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-software-cloud/docs/use-advanced-search-with-jira-query-language-jql/
last_updated: 2025-01-27
---
# Use advanced search with Jira Query Language (JQL)

JQL lets you build precise, structured searches that basic search can't express. You can use JQL in filters, on boards, in dashboards, and in automation rule conditions.

## Run an advanced search

1. Select **Filters** > **View all issues**.
2. Select **JQL** to switch from basic search.
3. Type your query. Jira suggests fields, operators, and values as you type.
4. Press **Enter** or select **Search**.

Search results only include issues you have the **Browse projects** permission for. Issue security levels can hide individual issues as well.

## Query structure

A simple query has a field, an operator, and a value, e.g. `status = "In Progress"`. You can join clauses with `AND` and `OR`, negate them with `NOT`, and sort results with `ORDER BY`. Values that contain spaces must be wrapped in quotes.

## Examples

Unresolved bugs assigned to you, newest first:

```
project = WEB AND issuetype = Bug AND assignee = currentUser() AND resolution = Unresolved ORDER BY created DESC
```

Issues updated in the last seven days:

```
updated >= -7d
```

> **Note:** Field names are not case-sensitive, but some values are, e.g. text in custom select lists created before 2023.

last_updated: 2024-12-11
---
# Add a transition to a workflow

A transition is a one-way link between two statuses. It appears as a button on the issue, e.g. **Start progress** or **Resolve**. To let issues move both ways between two statuses, add two transitions.

## Before you begin

You need the **Administer Jira** global permission to edit company-managed workflows. Changes go into a draft, so the live workflow keeps working until you publish.

## Add a transition

1. Go to **Settings** > **Issues** > **Workflows**.
2. Find the workflow and select **Edit**.
3. Select **Add transition**.
4. Choose the **From status** and **To status**, then enter a name.
5. Select **Add**.

## Add a condition or validator

Conditions decide who sees the transition. Validators check input before the transition runs, e.g. that **Fix versions** is set.

1. Select the transition, then select **Conditions** or **Validators**.
2. Select **Add condition** or **Add validator** and choose a type.
3. Configure it and select **Add**.

## Publish the workflow

1. Select **Publish draft**.
2. Choose whether to save a backup copy of the current version.
3. Select **Publish**.

> **Note:** If you remove a status that issues currently use, Jira asks you to map those issues to a new status before it publishes the draft.

title: Configure columns on a board
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-software-cloud/docs/configure-columns/
last_updated: 2025-01-14
---
# Configure columns on a board

Columns show where work is in your process. Each column on a company-managed board maps to one or more workflow statuses. When an issue moves to a status, the issue moves to the column that status is mapped to.

## Before you begin

You must be a board admin to change columns. If you aren't a board admin, the **Columns** page shows the configuration in read-only mode.

## Add or rename a column

1. Go to your board, then select **More** (•••) > **Board settings**.
2. Select **Columns**.
3. Select **Add column**, enter a name, and press **Enter**.
4. To rename a column, select its name and type over it.

Column names only change the board. They don't rename the underlying statuses.

## Map statuses to columns

Drag a status from the **Unmapped statuses** area into a column. A column can hold several statuses (e.g. **In review** and **Awaiting QA** under one **Review** column). Statuses left unmapped are hidden from the board, i.e. issues in those statuses won't appear anywhere on it.

> **Note:** The rightmost column is treated as done for reports such as the burndown chart. Map only your resolved statuses to it.

## Set column constraints

Constraints flag a column when it holds too few or too many issues.

1. In **Column constraint**, choose **Issue count** or **Issue count, excluding subtasks**.
2. Enter a minimum, a maximum, or both, at the bottom of each column.

A column turns red when it goes over its maximum and yellow when it falls under its minimum.

title: Create and edit Jira automation rules
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-cloud-administration/docs/create-and-edit-jira-automation-rules/
last_updated: 2025-02-25
---
# Create and edit Jira automation rules

Automation rules carry out routine work for you, e.g. assigning new bugs, closing parent issues when every subtask is done, or posting a comment when a due date passes.

## How rules are built

Every rule has a **trigger** that starts it, optional **conditions** that must pass, and one or more **actions** that make changes. Rules can be scoped to a single project, several projects, or globally. Only Jira admins can create multi-project and global rules.

## Create a rule

1. Go to **Project settings** > **Automation**.
2. Select **Create rule**.
3. Choose a trigger (e.g. **Issue created**) and select **Next**.
4. Add a condition such as **Issue fields condition**, then add an action.
5. Name the rule, then select **Turn it on**.

To edit a rule, select its name from the rules list, make your changes, and select **Save**.

## Use smart values

Smart values let an action insert data from the issue that triggered the rule. For example, this comment action addresses the reporter by name and shows the issue's priority:

```
Hi {{reporter.displayName}}, this issue is now {{issue.priority.name}} priority.
```

Smart values are case-sensitive, so `{{Issue.key}}` returns nothing where `{{issue.key}}` works.

## Check the audit log

Each rule keeps an audit log of its runs. Select **Audit log** to see whether a run succeeded, what it changed, and any errors.

> **Note:** Your plan's monthly limit on rule runs applies to single-project rules on Free and Standard plans. Check usage in **Automation** > **Usage**.

title: Create a notification scheme
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-cloud-administration/docs/create-a-notification-scheme/
last_updated: 2025-01-07
---
# Create a notification scheme

A notification scheme decides who receives email when something happens to an issue in a company-managed project, e.g. when it's created, assigned, commented on, or resolved. Each event in the scheme lists its recipients.

## Before you begin

You need the **Administer Jira** global permission. Recipients still need the **Browse projects** permission. Jira never emails people about issues they can't see.

## Create a scheme

1. Go to **Settings** > **Issues** > **Notification schemes**.
2. Select **Add notification scheme**.
3. Enter a name and description, then select **Add**.

A new scheme starts empty, i.e. no one is notified of anything until you add recipients. To start from the defaults, select **Copy** next to **Default Notification Scheme** instead.

## Add a notification

1. Next to the scheme, select **Notifications**.
2. Select **Add notification**.
3. Choose one or more events.
4. Choose a recipient type (e.g. **Current assignee**, **Reporter**, **Watchers**, or **Project role**).
5. Select **Add**.

## Associate the scheme with a project

1. Open the project and go to **Project settings** > **Notifications**.
2. Select **Actions** > **Use a different scheme**.
3. Choose the scheme and select **Associate**.

> **Note:** Users can turn off emails about their own changes in their personal settings. This preference overrides the scheme.

docs.body_markdown:

title: Use functions in JQL queries
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-software-cloud/docs/jql-functions/
last_updated: 2025-02-04
---
# Use functions in JQL queries

A JQL function returns a value that Jira works out when the query runs. You can save one filter that adjusts itself instead of editing dates, versions, or user names by hand.

## How functions work

Functions are written with a name followed by parentheses, e.g. `currentUser()` or `startOfWeek()`. Some take arguments, such as an offset for date functions or a project key for version functions. Function names aren't case-sensitive.

## Commonly used functions

- `currentUser()` returns the person running the search.
- `openSprints()` returns every sprint that has started but isn't complete.
- `startOfDay()`, `endOfWeek()`, and similar functions return a moment in time, with an optional offset such as `-1d` or `+2w`.
- `unreleasedVersions("KEY")` returns versions in a project that haven't been released.
- `membersOf("group-name")` returns every user in a group.

## Combine functions with operators

This query finds open work assigned to you in the current sprint that was updated in the past week:

```
assignee = currentUser() AND sprint in openSprints() AND statusCategory != Done AND updated >= startOfDay(-7d) ORDER BY priority DESC
```

Functions that return a list, i.e. more than one value, must be used with `in` or `not in` rather than `=`.

## Limitations

> **Note:** Date functions use the time zone set in your profile. A shared filter can return different results for teammates in other time zones.

Functions can't be nested, and each query is limited to 2,000 values returned from list functions such as `membersOf()`.

title: Configure Jira application options
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-cloud-administration/docs/configure-jira-application-options/
last_updated: 2025-01-09
---
# Configure Jira application options

General settings control how Jira behaves across your whole site, not inside a single project. They include the site title, the base URL shown in emails, the default language, and options such as voting and watching.

## Before you begin

You need the **Administer Jira** global permission. Some options, e.g. the base URL, are managed by Atlassian for cloud sites and appear read-only.

## Change general settings

1. Go to **Settings** > **System** > **General configuration**.
2. Select **Edit settings**.
3. Update the fields you want to change (e.g. **Title**, **Mode**, or **Maximum authentication attempts allowed**).
4. Select **Update**.

Changes apply as soon as you save. Users who already have Jira open may need to refresh the page.

## Set the default language and time zone

1. On the **General configuration** page, select **Edit settings**.
2. Under **Internationalization**, choose the **Default language** and **Default user time zone**.
3. Select **Update**.

> **Note:** These defaults only apply to people who haven't chosen their own language or time zone in their profile, i.e. a personal setting always wins.

## Options that affect every project

Turning off **Voting** or **Watching** hides those controls on every issue in every project. Existing votes and watchers are kept, so turning the option back on restores them. Disabling **Unassigned issues** requires every issue to have an assignee, which can block issue creation in projects with no default assignee.

title: Configure swimlanes on a board
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-software-cloud/docs/configure-swimlanes/
last_updated: 2024-12-11
---
# Configure swimlanes on a board

Swimlanes are horizontal rows on a board that group related issues. They help your team see work by person, by epic, or by any rule you define, without changing the columns that show workflow status.

## Swimlane types

Company-managed boards support grouping by **Queries**, **Stories**, **Assignees**, **Epics**, **Projects**, or **No swimlanes**. Team-managed boards offer a smaller set, i.e. epics, assignees, subtasks, or none.

## Change how swimlanes are grouped

1. Open the board and select **More** (•••) > **Board settings**.
2. Select **Swimlanes**.
3. Under **Base swimlanes on**, choose a grouping.

The board updates for everyone who uses it.

## Create query-based swimlanes

When you base swimlanes on queries, each row is defined by a JQL clause. For example, this swimlane collects urgent bugs:

```
priority in (Highest, High) AND issuetype = Bug
```

1. With **Queries** selected, enter a **Name**, a **JQL** clause, and an optional **Description**.
2. Select **Add**.

> **Note:** An issue appears only in the first swimlane whose query it matches. Issues that match no query fall into the **Everything else** swimlane at the bottom.

## Reorder or remove swimlanes

Drag a swimlane by its handle to change its position. To remove one, select **Delete** next to it. Removing a swimlane doesn't change any issues; they simply move to the next matching row.

title: Use smart values in automation rules
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-software-cloud/docs/what-are-smart-values/
last_updated: 2024-12-19
---
# Use smart values in automation rules

Smart values let an automation rule read data from the issue, the trigger, or the rule itself and insert it into an action. You can use them in comments, emails, field edits, and conditions.

## How smart values work

A smart value is written inside double curly braces, e.g. `{{issue.summary}}`. When the rule runs, Jira replaces it with the current value. Smart values are case-sensitive, so `{{Issue.Summary}}` returns nothing.

## Common smart values

- `{{issue.key}}` returns the issue key, such as `OPS-142`.
- `{{issue.assignee.displayName}}` returns the assignee's name.
- `{{initiator.displayName}}` returns the person whose action triggered the rule.
- `{{now}}` returns the date and time the rule ran.

## Format dates and text

You can chain functions onto a smart value. This comment adds a due date five business days from now:

```
Hi {{issue.reporter.displayName}}, we expect to resolve {{issue.key}} by {{now.plusBusinessDays(5).format("d MMMM yyyy")}}.
```

Text functions such as `.toUpperCase()` and `.abbreviate(50)` work the same way.

## Troubleshoot empty values

> **Note:** If a smart value refers to a field that is empty on the issue, Jira inserts nothing, i.e. no error appears in the audit log.

Use the **Log action** to print a smart value while you test a rule, then check the output in the rule's audit log before you enable it for the whole project.

title: Manage your personal notification settings
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-work-management/docs/manage-your-notification-settings/
last_updated: 2025-02-26
---
# Manage your personal notification settings

You can decide which Jira emails reach your inbox and how often they arrive. These settings only affect you; project admins control which events send notifications in the first place.

## Change your email notifications

1. Select your profile picture, then select **Settings**.
2. Under **Email notifications**, find the activity type (e.g. **Issues you're watching**, **Comments**, or **Mentions**).
3. Turn each switch on or off.

Your changes save automatically.

## Choose a batching option

Batching combines several updates to the same issue into one email. Under **Email notification format**, select **Send me a single email for multiple updates** to receive a summary roughly every 10 minutes instead of one email per change.

## Stop watching an issue

1. Open the issue.
2. Select the **Watch options** icon next to the issue actions.
3. Select **Stop watching**.

You can also unwatch from the link at the bottom of any notification email.

> **Note:** Mentions and direct assignments are always sent, i.e. turning off watching doesn't stop emails when someone adds `@yourname` to a comment.

## Why you still get some emails

If you keep receiving emails after turning a setting off, the project's notification scheme may include you through a group or role. Ask your project admin to check the scheme, or check whether your personal settings were changed in another browser session.

title: Edit multiple issues at the same time
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-software-cloud/docs/edit-multiple-issues-at-the-same-time/
last_updated: 2024-12-11
---
# Edit multiple issues at the same time

Bulk change lets you update many issues in one pass. You can edit fields, move issues to another project, transition them through a workflow, or delete them. This saves you from opening each issue on its own.

## Before you begin

You need the **Make bulk changes** global permission. You also need the relevant project permission for each issue in the selection, e.g. **Edit issues** to change fields or **Delete issues** to remove them. Jira skips any issue you don't have permission to change and lists it in the summary.

## Start a bulk change

1. Go to **Filters** > **View all issues**.
2. Run a search that returns the issues you want to change.
3. Select **More actions** (`•••`) > **Bulk change all issues**.
4. Select the checkbox next to each issue to include, then select **Next**.

## Choose a bulk operation

1. Choose one operation: **Edit issues**, **Move issues**, **Transition issues**, **Delete issues**, **Watch issues** or **Stop watching issues**.
2. Fill in the details for that operation. For example, choose the fields and new values for an edit.
3. Review the confirmation screen and select **Confirm**.

To avoid flooding watchers' inboxes, clear **Send mail for this update** before you confirm.

> **Note:** Transitioning issues in bulk only works when every selected issue uses the same workflow and the same transition, i.e. issues in different projects may need to be changed in separate batches.

## Limits on bulk changes

A single bulk change can include up to 1,000 issues. Larger operations run in the background, and you can follow their progress from the status page that opens after you confirm.

# Add conditions and validators to a workflow transition

Rules on a transition control who can move an issue between statuses and what has to be true first. Use them to enforce your team's process without relying on people to remember it.

## Conditions, validators and post functions

- **Conditions** decide whether a transition is shown to a user at all (e.g. only the assignee can select **Start progress**).
- **Validators** check the input when someone selects the transition, and block it if a check fails (e.g. a **Resolution** must be set).
- **Post functions** run after the transition completes, such as clearing a field or updating the assignee.

## Add a condition

1. Go to **Settings** > **Issues** > **Workflows** and select **Edit** next to the workflow.
2. Select the transition you want to restrict.
3. In the side panel, select **Add rule**, then choose **Restrict transition**.
4. Pick a condition, e.g. **Restrict to a user in a project role**, and select the role.
5. Select **Add**.

## Add a validator

1. With the transition selected, select **Add rule**.
2. Choose **Validate details**, then pick a rule such as **Field required** or **Field has been changed**.
3. Enter an error message that tells the user what to fill in.
4. Select **Add**.

> **Note:** A transition with several conditions only appears when all of them pass, i.e. conditions are combined with AND unless you group them with **Any of these rules**.

## Publish your changes

Workflow edits are saved as a draft. Select **Update workflow** to publish. If issues are in a status you removed, Jira asks you to map them to a new status before it saves.

title: Save your search as a filter

last_updated: 2025-02-04
---
# Save your search as a filter

A filter is a saved JQL search. Boards, dashboard gadgets and subscriptions all read from filters, so a well-named filter can be reused across your whole site.

## Save a filter

1. Go to **Filters** > **View all issues** and switch to JQL.
2. Enter your query, for example:

```
project = OPS AND status != Done AND assignee = currentUser() ORDER BY priority DESC
```

3. Select **Save as**, enter a name, and select **Save**.

Choose a name that describes the result, e.g. *OPS – my open work*, not the person who created it.

## Share a filter

1. Open the filter and select **Filter details** > **Edit permissions**.
2. Under **Viewers**, add a project, group or role.
3. Under **Editors**, add anyone who should be able to change the query.
4. Select **Save**.

Viewers still only see issues they already have permission to browse.

## Get a filter with the REST API

Scripts can read a saved filter through the Jira Cloud platform REST API v3:

```
GET /rest/api/3/filter/{id}
```

The response includes the `jql` string and the `searchUrl` you can call to run it.

## Change the filter owner

If the filter's owner leaves your organization, a Jira admin can reassign it. Go to **Settings** > **System** > **Filters**, find the filter, and select **Change owner**.

> **Note:** Deleting a filter breaks every board and gadget that uses it, i.e. check **Filter subscriptions** and board settings before you delete.

title: Configure time tracking
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-cloud-administration/docs/configure-time-tracking/
last_updated: 2024-12-17
---
# Configure time tracking

Time tracking lets people log the work they spend on an issue and compare it with the original estimate. The settings on this page apply to every project on your site.

## Before you begin

You need the **Administer Jira** global permission. If your site uses a time tracking app from the Atlassian Marketplace, that app may replace the built-in provider. Check **Time tracking provider** before you change anything.

## Turn time tracking on or off

1. Go to **Settings** > **Issues** > **Time tracking**.
2. Select **Activate** or **Deactivate**.

Deactivating hides the **Log work** action and time fields. It doesn't delete existing worklogs, so the data comes back if you activate it again.

## Set the working hours and time format

1. On the **Time tracking** page, enter **Working hours per day** (e.g. `8`) and **Working days per week** (e.g. `5`).
2. Choose a **Time format**: **pretty** (e.g. `2d 4h`), **days**, or **hours**.
3. Choose the **Default unit** used when someone enters a number with no unit.
4. Select **Save**.

> **Note:** Changing working hours changes how existing estimates are shown, i.e. a `1d` estimate becomes 7.5 hours if you change the day from 8 to 7.5 hours. Jira doesn't rewrite the stored values.

## Who can log work

Logging work needs the **Work on issues** project permission. Editing or deleting worklogs is controlled separately by the **Edit own worklogs**, **Edit all worklogs**, **Delete own worklogs** and **Delete all worklogs** permissions in each project's permission scheme.

title: Link issues to other issues

last_updated: 2025-02-11
---
# Link issues to other issues

Issue links show how two pieces of work relate to each other, e.g. one issue **blocks** another, **duplicates** it, or **relates to** it. Links work across projects on the same site, and each link type has an outward and an inward description, so the relationship reads correctly from both issues.

## Before you begin

You need the **Link issues** project permission in the project that holds the issue you're linking from. Your Jira admin must also have issue linking turned on in **Settings** > **Issues** > **Issue linking**.

## Link an issue

1. Open the issue you want to link from.
2. Select **Link issue** (the chain icon) below the summary.
3. Choose a link type, e.g. **is blocked by**.
4. Search for the issue by key or summary and select it.
5. Select **Link**.

The link appears in the **Linked issues** section of both issues.

## Remove an issue link

1. In the **Linked issues** section, hover over the link.
2. Select **Remove**, then confirm.

> **Note:** Removing a link only removes the relationship. Neither issue is changed in any other way, i.e. status, assignee and comments stay as they were.

## Find linked issues with JQL

Use the `linkedIssues()` function to list every issue linked to a given issue. Add a link type to narrow the results:

```
issue in linkedIssues("PROJ-123", "is blocked by")
```

This returns only the issues that block `PROJ-123`. You only see linked issues in projects you have the **Browse projects** permission for.

title: Use your Scrum backlog
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-software-cloud/docs/use-your-scrum-backlog/
last_updated: 2025-01-09
---
# Use your Scrum backlog

The backlog is where your team keeps the work it hasn't started yet and plans upcoming sprints. Every Scrum board has a backlog, and the issues it shows are the ones that match the board's filter but aren't in the done column.

## How the backlog is organized

The backlog has one section for each active or future sprint, followed by the **Backlog** section for unplanned work. Issues appear in rank order, i.e. the issue at the top is the one the team should pick up next.

## Rank issues in the backlog

1. Go to your Scrum project and select **Backlog**.
2. Drag an issue up or down to change its rank.
3. To move an issue straight to the top or bottom, select **More actions** (•••) > **Top of backlog** or **Bottom of backlog**.

Ranking needs the **Schedule issues** project permission, and the board's filter must be ordered by `Rank`.

## Plan a sprint from the backlog

1. Select **Create sprint**.
2. Drag issues from the **Backlog** section into the new sprint, or select several with **Shift** and drag them together.
3. Check the estimate total shown in the sprint header against your team's usual velocity.
4. Select **Start sprint** when you're ready.

> **Note:** You can only start a sprint if you have the **Manage sprints** permission for every project whose issues are in the board's filter.

## Hide or show the backlog

Team-managed projects can switch the backlog off. Go to **Project settings** > **Features** and turn **Backlog** off. Existing issues stay on the board, e.g. in the **To Do** column.

title: Configure outgoing email notifications

last_updated: 2025-01-14

# Configure outgoing email notifications

Jira sends email notifications when events happen on issues, e.g. an issue is created, assigned or commented on. Who gets each email is decided by the project's notification scheme. The settings on this page control whether email leaves your site at all and what it looks like when it arrives.

## Before you begin

You need the **Administer Jira** global permission. Changes apply to every project on the site.

## Turn outgoing email on or off

1. Go to **Settings** > **System** > **Outgoing email**.
2. Select **Disable outgoing mail** or **Enable outgoing mail**.

While outgoing mail is off, Jira doesn't queue notifications, i.e. events that happen during that time won't be emailed later when you switch it back on.

## Change the sender address

1. On the **Outgoing email** page, select **Edit settings**.
2. In **From address**, enter the address you want to use, e.g. `jira@yourcompany.com`.
3. Choose an **Email visibility** option to decide whether the actor's name appears in the sender field.
4. Select **Update**.

> **Note:** A custom sender domain must be verified in **admin.atlassian.com** before Jira can use it. Until then, emails are sent from `jira@yoursite.atlassian.net`.

## Check the mail queue

If people say they aren't receiving notifications, go to **Settings** > **System** > **Mail queue**. Items waiting in the queue are sent within a few minutes. Items in the error queue have failed, usually because the recipient address bounced. Ask the person to check their personal notification settings before you investigate further.

title: Configure workflow schemes

last_updated: 2025-03-03
---
# Configure workflow schemes

A workflow scheme maps each issue type in a company-managed project to the workflow it follows. For example, bugs can go through a review step that tasks skip, while both issue types still live in the same project.

## How workflow schemes work

Every scheme has a default workflow that applies to any issue type you haven't mapped explicitly. A scheme can be shared by several projects, so editing it changes all of them at once.

## Before you begin

You need the **Administer Jira** global permission. Team-managed projects manage workflows per issue type in **Project settings** and don't use workflow schemes.

## Assign a workflow to an issue type

1. Go to **Settings** > **Issues** > **Workflow schemes**.
2. Find the scheme and select **Edit**.
3. Select **Add workflow** > **Add existing**, choose the workflow, and select **Next**.
4. Select the issue types that should use it, e.g. **Bug** and **Incident**, then select **Finish**.
5. Select **Publish** to apply the draft.

> **Note:** If the new workflow doesn't contain every status your existing issues are in, Jira asks you to map the old statuses to new ones before it publishes, i.e. no issue is left in a status that the workflow doesn't have.

## Switch a project to a different workflow scheme

1. Open the project and go to **Project settings** > **Workflows**.
2. Select **Switch scheme**, choose the new scheme, and select **Associate**.
3. Map any statuses Jira asks about, then select **Associate** again.

Large projects can take several minutes to migrate. Keep the progress page open until it reports completion.

title: Create a custom field

last_updated: 2025-02-06

# Create a custom field

Custom fields capture information that Jira's built-in fields don't cover, e.g. a customer reference, a target release train, or a risk rating. In company-managed projects, a custom field is created once for the whole site and then made available to projects through field contexts and screens.

## Before you begin

You need the **Administer Jira** global permission. Every custom field adds to indexing and search load, so check whether an existing field already does the job before you add a new one.

## Add a custom field

1. Go to **Settings** > **Issues** > **Custom fields**.
2. Select **Create custom field**.
3. Choose a field type (e.g. **Select List (single choice)**, **Number Field**, or **Date Picker**) and select **Next**.
4. Enter a name and a description that tells people what to put in the field.
5. Select **Create**.

The field's ID appears in the URL of its configuration page, e.g. `customfield_10042`. You can use that ID in JQL with the syntax `cf[10042]`.

## Set the field context

A context controls which projects and issue types show the field, and which options and default value it has.

1. Next to the field, select **More** > **Contexts and default value**.
2. Select **Edit context**, then choose the projects and issue types it applies to.
3. Add options and a default value if the field type supports them.

> **Note:** A field with a global context appears in every project, i.e. it is searchable site-wide even where it isn't on a screen.

## Add the field to a screen

1. Go to **Settings** > **Issues** > **Screens**.
2. Find the screen your project uses and select **Configure**.
3. Select **Select Field**, search for the field, and add it.

The field now appears when people create, edit, or view issues that use that screen.

title: Run automation rules on a schedule
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-cloud-administration/docs/use-the-scheduled-trigger-in-automation/
last_updated: 2024-12-16
---
# Run automation rules on a schedule

The **Scheduled** trigger runs an automation rule at a fixed interval rather than in response to an event. Use it for housekeeping work, e.g. closing stale issues, sending a weekly reminder, or flagging overdue tasks every morning.

## How the scheduled trigger works

You set either a fixed rate (every N minutes, hours, or days) or a cron expression. Each run counts toward your site's monthly automation usage, whether or not the rule finds any issues to act on.

## Before you begin

You need the **Administer projects** permission to create a project rule, or the **Administer Jira** global permission to create a global or multi-project rule.

## Create a scheduled rule

1. Go to **Project settings** > **Automation** and select **Create rule**.
2. Select the **Scheduled** trigger.
3. Choose **Fixed rate interval** or **Cron expression**, then set the schedule.
4. Add the actions you want the rule to perform.
5. Name the rule and select **Turn it on**.

Cron expressions use six fields and the site's time zone. For example, the following runs at 08:00 on weekdays:

```
0 0 8 ? * MON-FRI
```

## Limit the rule with JQL

Select **Run a JQL search and execute actions for each issue in the query** so the rule only touches issues that match. For example:

```
project = OPS AND status = "Waiting for customer" AND updated <= -14d
```

Select **Only include issues that have changed since the last time this rule executed** to skip issues that the previous run already handled.

> **Note:** A single run processes up to 1,000 issues. If your query returns more, narrow it, i.e. split the rule by project or add a date clause.

title: Work with issues in the list view

last_updated: 2025-01-14
---
# Work with issues in the list view

The list view shows every issue in a business project as a row in a spreadsheet-style table. It's the quickest place to scan a large set of work, update several fields in a row, or spot issues that are missing an assignee or due date.

## About the list view

The list includes all issues in the project, not only those on the board, i.e. issues in every status appear here. Filters you apply at the top of the list are saved for you personally and don't change what teammates see.

## Edit issues inline

1. Open your project and select **List** from the navigation.
2. Select the cell you want to change, e.g. **Status**, **Assignee**, or **Due date**.
3. Enter or choose the new value. Changes save as soon as you leave the cell.

To create an issue, select **+ Create** at the bottom of the list, type a summary, and press `Enter`.

## Group and sort the list

1. Select **Group** and choose a field, e.g. **Status** or **Category**.
2. Expand or collapse each group to focus on part of the work.
3. Select a column header to sort by that field. Select it again to reverse the order.

> **Note:** Grouping by a custom field is only available for single-select and user picker fields.

## Show or hide columns

1. Select the **+** icon at the right end of the column headers.
2. Check the fields you want to display and clear the ones you don't.
3. Drag a column header to change its position.

Column choices are stored per user, so each person on the team can arrange the list the way they prefer.

title: Manage webhooks
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-cloud-administration/docs/manage-webhooks/
last_updated: 2025-03-05
---
# Manage webhooks

A webhook tells an external system when something happens in Jira, e.g. an issue is created, a comment is added, or a sprint starts. Jira sends an HTTP `POST` request with a JSON payload to the URL you register, so the other system doesn't need to poll for changes.

## Before you begin

You need the **Administer Jira** global permission. The receiving URL must be reachable over HTTPS from the public internet and should respond within 10 seconds.

## Register a webhook

1. Go to **Settings** > **System** > **WebHooks**.
2. Select **Create a WebHook**.
3. Enter a name and the URL that should receive events.
4. Select the events to send, e.g. **Issue: created** and **Issue: updated**.
5. Select **Create**.

You can also register webhooks with REST API version 3 by sending a request to `/rest/api/3/webhook`. Webhooks registered this way by an app expire after 30 days unless the app refreshes them.

## Filter events with JQL

Enter a JQL query to send events only for matching issues. For example:

```
project = SUP AND priority in (Highest, High)
```

Leave the query blank to send events for every issue the webhook's events apply to.

## Check the webhook payload

Each request includes the event name, a timestamp, and the affected issue. A trimmed example:

```json
{
  "timestamp": 1741171200000,
  "webhookEvent": "jira:issue_created",
  "issue": { "key": "SUP-128", "fields": { "summary": "Login page times out" } }
}
```

> **Note:** Jira retries a failed delivery up to five times, i.e. your endpoint can receive the same event more than once. Use the timestamp and issue key to discard duplicates.

title: Create a board
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-software-cloud/docs/create-a-board/
last_updated: 2025-01-09
---
# Create a board

A board displays issues from one or more projects as cards in columns, so your team can see work move from to-do to done. Company-managed projects can have several boards, e.g. one Scrum board for the development team and one Kanban board for support triage.

## Before you begin

To create a board, you need the **Create shared objects** global permission. You also need the **Browse projects** permission for every project the board will show. Team-managed projects come with a single board and don't support extra boards.

## Create a Scrum or Kanban board

1. From the navigation, select **Search** > **View all boards**.
2. Select **Create board**.
3. Choose **Scrum** if your team plans work in sprints, or **Kanban** if work flows continuously.
4. Select how the board should get its issues (see below).
5. Enter a board name and select **Create board**.

## Choose where the board gets its issues

You can base the board on an existing project or on a saved filter. A filter lets one board span several projects. For example:

```
project in (WEB, MOB) AND component = Checkout ORDER BY Rank ASC
```

Boards must be ordered by `Rank` for drag-and-drop ranking to work.

## Change the board filter later

Go to **Board settings** > **General** and select **Edit filter query**. The change applies to everyone who uses the board.

> **Note:** If a user can't see some issues in the filter, those cards are hidden for them only, i.e. the board can look different to different people.

title: Plan work in the calendar view
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-work-management/docs/use-the-calendar-view/
last_updated: 2024-12-16
---
# Plan work in the calendar view

The calendar view shows a business project's issues on the days they're due. It's useful for teams whose work is tied to dates, e.g. marketing campaigns, event planning, or month-end finance tasks.

## How the calendar view works

Each issue appears on its **Due date**. If the issue also has a **Start date**, the calendar shows it as a bar spanning both dates. Issues without a due date don't appear on the grid. The calendar is available in Jira Work Management projects and in team-managed software projects with the view turned on.

## Schedule an issue

1. Open the project and select **Calendar**.
2. Hover over a day and select **+ Create**, or drag an existing card to a new day.
3. Enter a summary and press **Enter**.

Dragging a card updates its due date immediately and is recorded in the issue's history.

## Filter the calendar

Use **Filter** to narrow the calendar by assignee, issue type, status, or label. You can also enter a search term to match issue summaries. Filters only apply to your view, i.e. they don't change what teammates see.

## Show unscheduled work

Select **Unscheduled** to open a side panel listing issues with no due date. Drag an issue from the panel onto a day to schedule it.

> **Note:** Issues you don't have permission to browse are never shown, even if they're due in the visible date range.

title: Add, edit, and delete an issue type
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-cloud-administration/docs/add-edit-and-delete-an-issue-type/
last_updated: 2025-01-14
---
# Add, edit, and delete an issue type

Issue types distinguish different kinds of work, e.g. **Bug**, **Task**, **Story**, or a custom type such as **Change request**. In company-managed projects, issue types are shared across the site and grouped into issue type schemes.

## Before you begin

You need the **Administer Jira** global permission. Changes to a shared issue type affect every project whose issue type scheme includes it.

## Add an issue type

1. Go to **Settings** > **Issues** > **Issue types**.
2. Select **Add issue type**.
3. Enter a name and description.
4. Choose **Standard issue type** or **Sub-task issue type**.
5. Select **Add**.

A new issue type isn't available to a project until you add it to that project's issue type scheme.

## Edit an issue type

Next to the issue type, select **More** (`•••`) > **Edit**. You can change its name, description, and avatar. Existing issues keep their data when you rename a type.

## Delete an issue type

1. Next to the issue type, select **More** (`•••`) > **Delete**.
2. If any issues use the type, choose a replacement issue type for them.
3. Select **Delete**.

> **Note:** Deleting an issue type can't be undone. If the replacement type uses a different workflow or field configuration, Jira asks you to map statuses and fields first, i.e. the migration may take several steps.

docs.title: Audit activities in Jira applications
docs.headings: ["Before you begin", "View the audit log", "Search and filter audit records", "Export audit records"]
docs.body_markdown:

title: Audit activities in Jira applications
source_url: https://support.atlassian.com/jira-cloud-administration/docs/audit-activities-in-jira-applications/
last_updated: 2025-02-26
---
# Audit activities in Jira applications

The audit log records administrative changes made on your Jira site, e.g. a permission scheme edit, a workflow publish, or a user being added to a group. Use it to find out who changed a setting and when.

## Before you begin

You need the **Administer Jira** global permission. Records are kept for a limited period that depends on your plan, so export anything you need to keep longer.

## View the audit log

1. Go to **Settings** > **System** > **Audit log**.
2. Select a record to see its details, including the author, the IP address, and the changed values.

Each record shows the old and new value side by side where Jira can capture them.

## Search and filter audit records

Enter a keyword such as a scheme name or a username, then narrow results by date range or category (e.g. **permissions**, **workflows**, **user management**). You can also read records with REST API version 3:

```
GET /rest/api/3/auditing/record?filter=permission&from=2025-02-01T00:00:00Z
```

## Export audit records

Select **Export** to download the current results as a CSV file. The export respects your filters, i.e. only matching records are included.

> **Note:** End-user actions such as viewing or editing an issue aren't recorded here. Check the issue's **History** tab for those changes.

title: Start a sprint

last_updated: 2025-01-14

# Start a sprint

Starting a sprint moves the planned issues out of the backlog and onto the board, where the team tracks them until the sprint is completed. Only Scrum boards have sprints. Kanban boards show work continuously instead.

## Before you begin

You need the **Manage sprints** permission for every project whose issues appear in the sprint. If even one issue belongs to a project where you don't hold that permission, the **Start sprint** button stays disabled.

## Start a sprint from the backlog

1. Go to your Scrum project and select **Backlog**.
2. Find the sprint you want to start. Make sure it contains at least one issue.
3. Select **Start sprint**.
4. Review the sprint name, duration, and dates, then select **Start**.

The board switches to the new sprint straight away, and the issues appear in the first column of the board.

## Set the sprint duration and goal

Choose a preset duration (e.g. **1 week**, **2 weeks**, **4 weeks**) or select **Custom** to enter exact start and end dates. Add a sprint goal that sums up what the team plans to deliver, e.g. "Ship the new invoice export". The goal appears at the top of the board and in the sprint report.

## Run more than one sprint at a time

To run sprints in parallel, a Jira admin must turn on **Parallel sprints** under **Settings** > **Products** > **Jira Software configuration**. The board then shows a sprint selector, i.e. each team member picks the sprint they want to view.

> **Note:** Changing the end date of an active sprint doesn't change the scope. Issues stay in the sprint until you complete it or move them back to the backlog.

# Add, edit, and delete resolutions

A resolution records why an issue stopped being worked on, e.g. **Done**, **Won't do**, or **Duplicate**. Resolutions are shared by every company-managed project on your site, so a change here affects all of them.

## How resolutions work

Jira treats any issue with a resolution value as resolved, whatever its status. Reports, filters, and the `resolution = Unresolved` JQL clause all depend on this field, i.e. an issue in a Done status with an empty resolution still counts as open.

## Add a resolution

1. Go to **Settings** > **Issues** > **Resolutions**.
2. Select **Add resolution**.
3. Enter a name and a description that explains when to use it.
4. Select **Add**.

Use **Set as default** to choose which resolution appears first when people resolve an issue.

## Edit or delete a resolution

Select **Edit** next to a resolution to rename it. Renaming keeps the value on existing issues. To delete a resolution, select **Delete** and choose a replacement. Jira moves every issue that used the old value to the replacement.

## Set the resolution on a transition

Add a **Resolve issue** screen to the transition into your final status, or add a post function that sets the field automatically:

```
Update issue field: Resolution = Done
```

On transitions that reopen an issue, add a post function that clears the resolution.

> **Note:** Team-managed projects set the resolution automatically when an issue moves to a status in the Done category, so you can't configure it per transition.

# Manage notifications in team-managed projects

Team-managed projects don't use notification schemes. Each project has its own notification settings, which the project admin controls directly from the project.

## Before you begin

You need the **Administrator** role in the team-managed project. Jira admins can also change these settings for any project on the site.

## Change who gets notified

1. Go to your project and select **Project settings** > **Notifications**.
2. Find the event you want to change (e.g. **Issue created**, **Issue assigned**, **Comment added**).
3. Select **Edit**.
4. Add or remove recipients, such as **Reporter**, **Assignee**, **All watchers**, or a specific role.
5. Select **Save**.

Changes apply to the next notification Jira sends. Emails that are already queued aren't affected.

## Turn off a notification event

To stop a notification for everyone in the project, edit the event and remove every recipient. Individual users can still mute notifications for themselves in their personal settings.

## How team-managed notifications differ

In a company-managed project, several projects can share one notification scheme. In a team-managed project, the settings belong to that project only, i.e. editing them never changes another project. Custom events created for company-managed schemes aren't available here.

> **Note:** Users only receive a notification if they can see the issue. A recipient who loses access to the project, e.g. after being removed from the project's roles, stops getting emails about its issues.

# View the audit log for an automation rule

Every time an automation rule runs, Jira writes an entry to the rule's audit log. The entry shows what triggered the rule, which issues it touched, and whether each action succeeded. Check this log first when a rule doesn't behave as expected.

## Before you begin

Project admins can view audit logs for rules in their own projects. You need the **Administer Jira** global permission to view logs for global and multi-project rules.

## Open a rule's audit log

1. Go to **Project settings** > **Automation**, or **Settings** > **System** > **Global automation**.
2. Select the rule.
3. Select **Audit log** in the rule details panel.
4. Expand an entry to see the trigger, the conditions checked, and each action's result.

## Understand rule statuses

Each entry has a status, e.g. **Success**, **No actions performed**, **Some errors**, or **Throttled**. **No actions performed** usually means a condition failed, i.e. the rule ran correctly but had nothing to do.

## Debug a failing rule

Add a **Log action** to write smart values into the audit log while you test:

```
{{issue.key}} moved to {{issue.status.name}} by {{initiator.displayName}}
```

Run the rule again, then compare the logged values with what you expected. Remove the log action once the rule works.

> **Note:** Audit log entries are kept for 90 days. Entries for rules you delete are removed along with the rule.

# Customize the look and feel of Jira

You can brand your Jira site so it matches your organization's identity. Changes to the logo, site title, and colors apply to everyone who uses the site, including people who only reach it through shared links or email notifications.

## Before you begin

You need the **Administer Jira** global permission. Project avatars are managed separately in each project's settings, so the steps below don't change them.

## Change the site logo and title

1. Go to **Settings** > **System** > **Look and feel**.
2. Under **Site logo**, select **Upload logo** and choose a PNG or SVG file.
3. Enter a **Site title**. The title appears in browser tabs and in the header of notification emails.
4. Select **Save**.

We recommend a logo with a transparent background that is at least 64 pixels high, so it stays sharp on high-density displays.

## Change the default color scheme

1. On the **Look and feel** page, select **Edit colors**.
2. Enter a hex value (e.g. `#0052CC`) for the navigation bar, or select **Extract from logo** to let Jira suggest colors.
3. Select **Save** to apply the scheme.

> **Note:** Users who choose dark or light mode in their personal settings still see your brand colors in the navigation bar, i.e. the theme setting only changes the page background and text.

## Reset to the default theme

Select **Reset to default** on the **Look and feel** page to restore the Atlassian logo and colors. This can't be undone, so download your current logo first if you might need it again.

# Configure quick filters on a board

Quick filters narrow the issues shown on a board without changing the board's own filter. Each quick filter is a JQL clause that appears as a button above the board, and people can turn several on at once to combine them.

## Before you begin

You need to be a board admin to add or change quick filters. Quick filters are available on company-managed Scrum and Kanban boards.

## Add a quick filter

1. Go to your board, then select **More** (•••) > **Board settings**.
2. Select **Quick filters**.
3. Enter a **Name** and the **JQL** for the filter.
4. Optionally, add a **Description**. It shows as a tooltip on the button.
5. Select **Add**.

The new filter appears at the end of the list. Drag it to change where it sits on the board.

## Example quick filters

Quick filters accept any valid JQL clause, e.g. issues updated recently or bugs assigned to nobody:

```
updated >= -1d
```

```
issuetype = Bug AND assignee is EMPTY
```

> **Note:** When more than one quick filter is active, Jira joins them with `AND`, i.e. an issue must match every active filter to stay on the board.

## Edit or delete a quick filter

On the **Quick filters** page, select **Edit** next to a filter to change its name or JQL, or select **Delete** to remove it. Deleting a quick filter removes it for everyone who uses the board.

# Track project progress in the summary view

The summary view gives a quick picture of how work in a business project is going. It collects status, priority, and workload information into a set of cards, so you can spot problems without building a dashboard or writing a filter.

## Open the summary view

1. Open your business project.
2. Select **Summary** in the project navigation.

If you don't see **Summary**, a project admin may have hidden it. They can turn it back on from **Project settings** > **Features**.

## What the summary view shows

The view includes cards for status overview, priority breakdown, types of work, team workload, and recent activity. Counts include every issue in the project that you have permission to see, i.e. issues restricted by an issue security level are left out for people who can't view them.

## Filter the summary view

1. Select **Filter** at the top of the page.
2. Choose a time range (e.g. **Last 7 days** or **Last 30 days**).
3. Optionally, narrow the view by assignee or type of work.

The filter applies to all cards at once and resets when you leave the page.

> **Note:** The summary view refreshes about every 5 minutes. Changes you make to issues may not appear right away.

## Share a summary with your team

Copy the page URL from your browser and share it. People who open the link see the view with their own permissions applied, so their numbers may differ from yours.
